sections.preview: Writers adjust vocabulary, detail, tone, organization, headings, and examples for readers and purpose. Accessible classroom materials use clear language, visible structure, defined acronyms, and required actions at the point of need. These supports can improve access without lowe
sections.content: Writers adjust vocabulary, detail, tone, organization, headings, and examples for readers and purpose. Accessible classroom materials use clear language, visible structure, defined acronyms, and required actions at the point of need. These supports can improve access without lowering the intellectual goal. Follow accommodations and educator plans, and avoid assuming that language difference or disability determines the students ideas.

expandableCase.label: Applied instructional-support case
expandableCase.title: Supporting Audience-Aware Writing and Documented 504 Accommodations
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: During a teacher-designed fifth-grade task to write a recycling guide for first graders, one student with a 504 plan for written expression freezes at a blank page, while a peer drafts a dense paragraph packed with unexplained acronyms like "MRF" and adult-level policy jargon.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Provide the 504-approved organizer and speech-to-text for independent drafting, and coach the peer to use plain language and clear headings.
expandableCase.explanation: Implementing documented accommodations removes transcription barriers while maintaining grade-level writing expectations, and adapting vocabulary and structure to first graders builds genuine audience awareness. Drafting sentences for the stalled student removes ownership, and overlooking jargon leaves the guide inaccessible.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A draft has weak organization and several comma errors. What should generally be addressed first?
choices: One comma only
Handwriting color
Alphabetical paragraph order
Overall structure and logic
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Higher-level revision should precede final editing because changes to organization may move, combine, or remove sentences.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: During writing support, what makes instructional feedback transferable to future drafts?
choices: It names a goal, text line, effect, and reusable step.
It rewrites every rough sentence directly for the author.
It gives a single numeric score without written comments.
It centers on personal style tastes outside the rubric.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Specific strategy-based feedback helps the student make the current change and apply the same reasoning in future writing.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: When coaching a young writer on a narrative draft, which question best supports elaboration?
choices: Can you repeat the word messy five times in a row?
Which sights, sounds, or actions picture the scene?
Should we delete the entire story setting instead?
Can you add a fact about an unrelated tall building?
knowledgeChecks.rationale: The prompt requests concrete relevant detail that allows the writer to show the condition rather than merely label it.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: How should support preserve student authorship?
choices: Draft the polished final paragraph directly for the child.
Require the student to adopt the adult’s preferred view.
Offer models and prompts while the learner owns wording.
Replace the writing assignment with unrelated worksheets.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Scaffolding supports the process but keeps the learner responsible for meaning, evidence, and final expression.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Which change most improves an acronym-heavy family notice?
choices: Insert extra formal school abbreviations into the letter.
Place required family steps inside a tiny bottom footnote.
Merge every school announcement into one unbroken block.
Define acronyms, add headings, and state actions clearly.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Defined terms, clear hierarchy, and direct action language improve navigation and comprehension for a varied audience.

chapterTakeaways: Match writing support to the teacher's current stage—graphic organizers for planning, oral rehearsal for drafting, content prompts for revising, and checklists for final editing.
Preserve student authorship by modeling techniques on a separate example and asking guiding questions rather than rewriting a student's sentences or substituting your own voice.
Give concrete, transferable feedback focused on one or two teacher-selected rubric priorities while supporting approved accessibility tools like word banks or speech-to-text.

diagrams.title: Reading Skills & Comprehension Support Routine
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Guide students through structured reading comprehension support by previewing vocabulary and text features, distinguishing main ideas from supporting details, prompting context-clue and inference checks, and building evidence-based summaries.
diagrams.caption: An original classroom-support flow sequencing text-feature preview, main-idea versus detail verification, context-clue and inference prompting, and text-anchored summarizing for ParaPro (1755).

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right reading support routine from previewing vocabulary and text features through verifying main idea versus supporting details and guiding context-clue/inference checks to summarizing with text evidence.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, preview key vocabulary, headings, captions, charts, and text organization with students before reading so they know what to look for. Second, help students verify the central main idea and separate it from individual supporting facts, examples, or personal opinions. Third, prompt students to use surrounding context clues, word parts, and explicit textual clues to test inferences rather than guessing from background knowledge alone. Fourth, guide students to state an accurate, objective summary in their own words grounded in key text evidence, looping back to exact sentences whenever a detail or meaning is unclear.
textEquivalent: Preview Vocabulary & Text Features: Scan headings, subheadings, bold terms, visuals, and glossary cues with the student to activate purpose and pre-teach high-utility words before reading.

Verify Main Idea vs. Supporting Details: Ask what the whole passage or section is mostly about and have the student point to specific facts or examples that support—rather than replace—that central idea.

Guide Context-Clue & Inference Checks: Prompt students to examine surrounding sentences, prefixes/roots, and textual clues ("What line makes you think that?") so inferences remain grounded in the passage.
Summarize Accurately with Text Evidence: Coach students to combine the main idea and essential supporting points concisely in their own words without adding opinions or unsupported details.

nodes.label: Preview Vocabulary & Text Features
nodes.detail: Walk through titles, headings, captions, diagrams, and key unfamiliar words before reading so students anticipate structure and meaning.

nodes.label: Verify Main Idea vs. Details
nodes.detail: Help students distinguish the overarching message from isolated facts or examples by checking whether each detail actually supports the main idea.

nodes.label: Guide Context & Inference Checks
nodes.detail: Prompt learners to use surrounding sentence clues, word parts (prefixes, roots, suffixes), and "show me in the text" questions to justify inferences.

nodes.label: Summarize Using Text Evidence
nodes.detail: Support students in crafting a brief, accurate summary in their own words that captures key ideas while excluding minor trivia or personal opinions.

edges.label: frames text structure to locate the central idea
uses verified facts to anchor word meaning and inference

diagrams.title: Inference Verification & Context-Clue Coaching Flow
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Support students in making evidence-based inferences and unlocking unfamiliar vocabulary by gathering explicit textual clues, weighing competing conclusions against overstatements, combining context clues with word parts, and modeling structured think-aloud reasoning.
diagrams.caption: An original classroom-support flow linking textual clue collection, competing-inference checks, context and word-part decoding, and think-aloud coaching for ParaPro (1755).

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right inference and vocabulary coaching flow from gathering explicit textual clues through testing competing conclusions and decoding context clues and word parts to modeling think-aloud support.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, help the student locate exact textual clues—words, character actions, facts, or multimodal captions—before jumping to an unstated conclusion. Second, test competing conclusions side by side so students choose the supported inference and reject overstatements or unsupported outside assumptions. Third, unpack unfamiliar vocabulary by pairing surrounding context clues (definitions, examples, or contrasts) with prefixes, roots, and suffixes to confirm precise meaning in the sentence. Fourth, reinforce independent habits through brief teacher-aligned think-alouds that name the clue type and ask the student to point back to specific lines whenever an answer feels like a guess.
textEquivalent: Gather Explicit Textual Clues: Ask the student to locate exact lines, actions, facts, or visual captions that serve as concrete evidence before forming any inference.
Compare & Test Competing Conclusions: Weigh plausible interpretations against the passage so students spot supported conclusions and eliminate extreme overstatements or unsupported assumptions.
Use Context Clues & Word Parts: Combine surrounding sentence clues (synonyms, contrasts, examples) with prefixes, roots, and suffixes to verify word meaning inside the passage.
Coach with Think-Aloud Prompts: Model naming the clue type aloud and prompt students to justify their reasoning with text evidence rather than guessing or receiving the answer.

nodes.label: Gather Explicit Textual Clues
nodes.detail: Anchor inference work in concrete wording, dialogue, facts, or multimodal captions directly visible in the passage before adding reasoning.

nodes.label: Test Competing Conclusions
nodes.detail: Compare candidate conclusions against passage evidence to distinguish warranted inferences from overstatements or unsupported outside assumptions.

nodes.label: Use Context Clues & Word Parts
nodes.detail: Pair surrounding context clues (definition, example, contrast) with prefixes, roots, and suffixes to determine accurate word meaning in context.

nodes.label: Coach with Think-Aloud Prompts
nodes.detail: Model how to name the clue type aloud and prompt students to point to supporting lines so they practice independent inferential reasoning.

edges.label: grounds every candidate conclusion in observable text evidence
clarifies unfamiliar words that shape subtle meaning
turns clue-finding steps into reusable student prompts
redirects guesswork back to specific sentences in the text

diagrams.title: Text Structure, Features & Source-Comparison Routine
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Help students read informational texts and multiple sources strategically by recognizing organizational patterns, navigating headings and data displays, comparing primary versus secondary viewpoints, and organizing evidence in graphic organizers or source matrices.
diagrams.caption: An original classroom-support flow connecting organizational pattern recognition, text-feature and data-display navigation, primary-versus-secondary source comparison, and graphic-organizer scaffolding for ParaPro (1755).

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right informational reading support flow from identifying organizational patterns through using text features and data displays and comparing primary versus secondary sources to scaffolding analysis with graphic organizers and source matrices.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, help students spot the text’s organizational pattern—sequence, cause and effect, comparison and contrast, or problem and solution—by highlighting transition words and paragraph layout. Second, guide students to use text features such as headings, glossaries, captions, labels, and chart scales to locate key information and read visual data accurately. Third, coach students to compare multiple sources by distinguishing firsthand primary records from later secondary interpretations while checking viewpoint and credibility. Fourth, reinforce comprehension with teacher-chosen graphic organizers or source matrices that mirror the passage’s structure, looping back to organizational cues whenever students are unsure where information belongs.
textEquivalent: Identify Organizational Patterns: Coach students to spot signal words and structural relationships for sequence, cause and effect, comparison, and problem-solution passages.
Use Text Features & Data Displays: Direct students to headings, glossaries, captions, and graph scales so they locate facts efficiently and interpret embedded visuals without misreading units.
Compare Viewpoints & Source Types: Help learners separate firsthand primary sources from secondary accounts while examining author perspective, purpose, and credibility across texts.
Scaffold with Organizers & Matrices: Support students in recording structured evidence on teacher-aligned graphic organizers or source matrices that reflect the text’s organization.

nodes.label: Identify Organizational Patterns
nodes.detail: Use signal words and layout cues to recognize sequence, cause and effect, comparison, or problem-and-solution structures across informational texts.

nodes.label: Use Text Features & Data Displays
nodes.detail: Guide students through headings, glossaries, captions, and chart scales so they locate facts quickly and interpret visual data accurately.

nodes.label: Compare Sources & Viewpoints
nodes.detail: Distinguish firsthand primary evidence from secondary interpretations while evaluating viewpoint, supporting details, and source credibility.

nodes.label: Scaffold with Organizers & Matrices
nodes.detail: Use teacher-planned graphic organizers and source-comparison matrices so students sort details, viewpoints, and evidence systematically.

edges.label: pairs overall text organization with headings and charts
surfaces author details, captions, and data for source evaluation
records cross-source similarities, differences, and credibility notes
reinforces how the chosen organizer matches the text pattern

diagrams.title: Supporting Foundational Reading & Decoding in Small Groups
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Deliver teacher-planned small-group foundational reading practice using phonemic cues, systematic letter-sound and syllable prompts, echo or choral reading for fluency, and objective progress notes for the licensed teacher.
diagrams.caption: An original classroom-support flow covering phonemic cues, decoding and syllable prompts, fluency modeling via echo/choral reading, and objective observation handoff to the teacher.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right small-group decoding support flow from phonemic blending and segmenting cues through systematic letter-sound and syllable prompts and echo/choral fluency practice to objective observation notes for the teacher.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, reinforce oral phonemic awareness using brief, teacher-assigned blending and segmenting cues (stretching and tapping individual sounds cleanly without adding extra schwa sounds). Second, when a student stalls on an unfamiliar print word, give systematic letter-sound, phonics-pattern, and syllable-chunking prompts instead of telling the student to guess from pictures or immediately supplying the word. Third, build accurate pacing, expression, and phrasing through structured echo reading, choral reading, or brief partner rereading of accessible text. Fourth, record specific, objective observations—such as which phonics patterns or multisyllabic words tripped up the student—and share them with the licensed teacher to inform instructional planning without diagnosing a disability or replacing core instruction.
textEquivalent: Phonemic Blending & Segmenting Cues: Lead brief teacher-planned oral sound activities—blending spoken phonemes into words and segmenting words into clean individual sounds using finger taps or sound boxes.

Systematic Letter-Sound & Syllable Prompts: Coach students to look through the entire word, blend known letter-sound correspondences, and break longer words into manageable syllables or morphemes rather than guessing from pictures.

Echo & Choral Reading for Phrasing: Model smooth rate, phrasing, and punctuation-guided expression, then guide students through echo reading, choral reading, and brief corrective rereading to build automaticity.

Record Objective Observations for Teacher Planning: Log concrete notes on mastered patterns, recurring decoding errors, and prompt level needed so the classroom teacher can adjust groups and instruction—never diagnosing or redesigning core curricula independently.

nodes.label: Phonemic Blending & Segmenting Cues
nodes.detail: Reinforce oral phoneme blending and segmenting with clean sound articulation and tactile cues (tapping, sound boxes) aligned to the teacher’s lesson sequence.

nodes.label: Letter-Sound & Syllable Prompts
nodes.detail: Prompt students to track print left-to-right, sound out phonics patterns, and chunk prefixes, roots, or syllables instead of guessing from illustrations or skipping words.

nodes.label: Echo & Choral Reading for Phrasing
nodes.detail: Model fluent phrasing and expression with echo reading, choral reading, and short rereads of decoded sentences to connect accurate word reading with comprehension.

nodes.label: Objective Notes for Teacher Planning
nodes.detail: Document specific patterns mastered, error types, and support needed for the licensed teacher’s planning—never diagnosing disabilities or independently altering core reading programs.

edges.label: connects oral speech sounds to printed spelling patterns
applies accurate word decoding inside connected sentences
captures accuracy, phrasing, and error patterns objectively
informs teacher-directed focus for the next small-group session

diagrams.title: Mathematics Computation & Word-Problem Support Pathway
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Help students unpack mathematics computation and word problems step by step by identifying known values and goals, modeling with place value, fractions, decimals, or ratios, coaching step-by-step calculation, and checking reasonableness and units.
diagrams.caption: An original classroom-support flow guiding problem unpacking, numerical representation, student-led calculation, and reasonableness and unit verification for ParaPro (1755).

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right math support pathway from identifying known quantities and question goal through modeling with place value, fractions, decimals, or ratios and guiding step-by-step calculation to checking reasonableness and units.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, help the student read the problem carefully, restate what the question is asking in plain words, and list known quantities and units while filtering out extraneous numbers. Second, connect the problem to the teacher’s math model—such as place-value columns, fraction bars, decimal alignment, or ratio tables—so operation choices come from meaning rather than blind keyword tricks. Third, coach the student through step-by-step computation while keeping the pencil in the student’s hand, prompting neat alignment, order of operations, and regrouping or common-denominator checks. Fourth, prompt the student to estimate before or after calculating and verify whether the answer’s size, sign, and measurement units make sense in the original story, revisiting the model if an error appears.
textEquivalent: Identify Known Quantities & Question Goal: Ask the student to retell the problem in their own words, highlight given values with units, and state clearly what quantity must be found.

Model with Place Value, Fractions, Decimals or Ratios: Represent relationships visually or structurally (place-value charts, fraction strips, number lines, or ratio tables) so students choose operations from meaning rather than isolated keywords.

Guide Step-by-Step Student Calculation: Keep the student doing the writing and thinking while prompting clean place-value or decimal alignment, common denominators, order of operations, and accurate regrouping.

Check Reasonableness & Measurement Units: Ask the student to compare the answer with a quick rounded estimate, verify the correct unit label (such as inches, dollars, or square feet), and confirm the result answers the exact question.

nodes.label: Identify Knowns & Question Goal
nodes.detail: Have the student restate the scenario, list given numbers with units, filter extra details, and define exactly what the final answer must represent.

nodes.label: Model Place Value, Fractions or Ratios
nodes.detail: Map quantities using teacher-taught models—place-value charts, fraction bars, decimal grids, number lines, or ratio tables—rather than relying on fragile keyword shortcuts.

nodes.label: Guide Step-by-Step Calculation
nodes.detail: Coach student-led computation with focused prompts on decimal/place-value alignment, equivalent fractions, order of operations, and keeping intermediate steps organized.

nodes.label: Check Reasonableness & Units
nodes.detail: Prompt a quick rounded estimate to catch decimal-shift or operation errors, confirm the correct measurement unit, and check the answer back against the story.

edges.label: translates problem facts into a concrete numerical structure
selects valid operations grounded in quantitative meaning
tests computed result for realistic size and correct unit label
revisits representation when an estimate reveals a setup error

diagrams.title: Ratios, Expressions & Equation-Balance Support Flow
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Guide students through proportional and introductory algebraic reasoning on ParaPro (1755) by preserving multiplicative relationships in ratios and unit rates, simplifying expressions with distributive and like-term rules, solving equations as balanced scales, and coaching through common errors.
diagrams.caption: An original classroom-support flow linking ratio/unit-rate reasoning, expression simplification, equation balance with inverse operations, and error-analysis coaching for ParaPro (1755).

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right algebra support flow from building ratios and unit rates through simplifying expressions with properties and solving equations as a balance to spotting common errors and coaching multiplicative reasoning.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, build equivalent ratios and per-one unit rates multiplicatively using ratio tables or double number lines, helping students see why adding the same constant to both parts breaks proportionality. Second, simplify algebraic expressions by applying the distributive property to every term inside parentheses and combining only like terms with matching variables and exponents. Third, treat every equation as a balanced scale: apply the same inverse operation to both sides step by step to isolate the variable, then substitute the solution back into the original equation to verify equality. Fourth, analyze recurring errors—such as additive shortcuts, dropped signs, or unbalanced operations—and prompt students back to the ratio or balance model rather than simply telling them the answer.
textEquivalent: Build Ratios & Unit Rates: Scale both quantities multiplicatively via ratio tables or unit rates (value per one unit) instead of adding equal amounts to each term.
Simplify Expressions with Properties: Distribute factors across every term inside parentheses and combine only like terms that share the same variable and power.
Solve Equations as a Balance: Keep both sides of the equals sign balanced by applying identical inverse operations to isolate the variable, then verify by substitution.
Spot Common Errors & Coach Meaning: Diagnose additive-ratio slips, distribution omissions, or one-sided steps through guiding questions that return the learner to visual models.

nodes.label: Ratios & Unit Rates
nodes.detail: Model equivalent ratios and per-one unit rates using multiplicative scaling in ratio tables so students avoid additive reasoning errors.

nodes.label: Expressions & Properties
nodes.detail: Apply the distributive property cleanly across parenthetical terms and combine only like terms before attempting to solve.

nodes.label: Equations as Balance
nodes.detail: Preserve equality by applying the same inverse operation to both sides step by step, then substitute the result back to verify the solution.

nodes.label: Error Analysis & Coaching
nodes.detail: Identify misconceptions—additive ratio shifts, missed distribution, or unbalanced steps—and prompt students to test their work against the balance model.

edges.label: links proportional scaling rules to symbolic expressions
simplifies each side cleanly before isolating the unknown
uses substitution checks to surface sign or balance slips
rebuilds multiplicative reasoning when additive habits appear

diagrams.title: Geometry Measurement, Coordinates & Unit-Conversion Flow
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Help students solve geometry and measurement tasks accurately on ParaPro (1755) by classifying whether a task asks for perimeter, area, or volume, connecting formulas to perpendicular base and height, reading angles and coordinate grids accurately, and converting units consistently.
diagrams.caption: An original classroom-support flow sequencing attribute classification, meaningful formula selection, angle/coordinate reading, and unit-conversion verification for ParaPro (1755).

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right geometry support flow from identifying what attribute is measured through applying formulas with base and height and reading angles and coordinates to converting units and checking dimensions.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, help the student determine what physical attribute is being measured—distance around a boundary (perimeter in linear units), flat surface covered (area in square units), or space inside a solid (volume in cubic units)—before picking a formula. Second, connect each formula to its geometric meaning using perpendicular base and height measurements so students understand why square or cubic units emerge. Third, guide accurate diagram reading for right and straight angles as well as plotting or reading ordered pairs (x, y) on the coordinate plane (horizontal first, then vertical). Fourth, convert mixed measurements into one shared unit using conversion factors before calculating, then re-check the final unit and dimension against what the problem requested.
textEquivalent: Identify What Is Being Measured: Clarify whether the problem asks for 1D boundary distance (perimeter), 2D surface coverage (area), or 3D interior capacity (volume) before selecting a formula.
Connect Formulas to Base & Height: Match perpendicular base and height dimensions to the correct formula and label outputs accurately in linear, square, or cubic units.
Read Angles & Coordinate Grids: Use straight-angle (180-degree) and right-angle (90-degree) relationships on figures and read or plot (x, y) ordered pairs horizontally first, then vertically.
Convert Units & Check Dimensions: Unify mixed measurement units with conversion factors prior to computing, then verify the final unit label matches the requested dimension.

nodes.label: What Is Being Measured
nodes.detail: Determine whether the task asks for boundary length (perimeter, 1D), surface coverage (area, 2D), or interior capacity (volume, 3D) before choosing a formula.

nodes.label: Formulas with Meaning
nodes.detail: Connect formulas to perpendicular base and height dimensions and match answers to linear, square, or cubic units rather than memorizing isolated letters.

nodes.label: Angles & Coordinates
nodes.detail: Apply straight-angle and right-angle facts on labeled figures and read or plot (x, y) ordered pairs across the coordinate plane in exact horizontal-then-vertical order.

nodes.label: Units & Conversions
nodes.detail: Convert mixed side lengths into a single shared unit with conversion factors before calculating, then verify that the final unit matches the required dimension.

edges.label: selects the matching 1D, 2D, or 3D formula family
uses angle cues and grid coordinates to confirm base and height
aligns all diagram lengths to one consistent measurement unit
re-checks linear, square, or cubic labels against the prompt

diagrams.title: Assisting Students with Visual Math Representations & Data Graphs
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Support students in reading data displays and connecting multiple math representations—tables, graphs, manipulatives, area models, and equations—while prompting student reasoning instead of giving away answers.
diagrams.caption: An original classroom-support flow linking graph-feature orientation, cross-representation translation, concrete/area modeling, and student-explanation prompting.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right visual math support flow from reading titles, axis labels, and unit intervals through translating between tables, graphs, and equations and using manipulatives or area models to prompting student explanation.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, orient students to every structural element of a chart or graph—title, horizontal and vertical axis labels, scale intervals, keys, and symbols—so they do not misread a scale of 2, 5, or 10 as 1. Second, help students translate the same mathematical relationship across tables, bar or line graphs, coordinate grids, and symbolic equations to see how each display shows patterns, totals, or rates of change. Third, bridge abstract concepts with concrete manipulatives, fraction strips, base-ten blocks, or area models aligned to the teacher’s approach so learners see why procedures work. Fourth, ask open-ended explanation prompts ("How did you read that bar?" or "Where do you see that number in the table?") rather than supplying answers, reinforcing conceptual ownership and noting any lingering misconceptions for the teacher.
textEquivalent: Read Title, Axis Labels & Unit Intervals: Have students identify what each axis measures, how much each grid step or pictograph symbol represents, and what the key or legend indicates before answering any data question.

Translate Across Tables, Graphs & Equations: Guide students to match data pairs between frequency tables, bar/line graphs, coordinate plots, and equations so they connect visual trends to exact numerical values.

Use Concrete Manipulatives & Area Models: Provide teacher-approved visual scaffolds—such as base-ten blocks, counters, fraction tiles, tape diagrams, or area models—to make operations, fractions, and geometry formulas tangible.

Prompt Student Explanation Over Answer-Giving: Use probing questions ("How do you know?", "Can you show that on the graph?") and allow wait time so the student explains their reasoning instead of passively copying a paraprofessional’s answer.

nodes.label: Read Title, Axes & Unit Intervals
nodes.detail: Guide students to inspect the chart title, x- and y-axis labels, interval increments (such as counting by 2s or 5s), and symbol keys before reading values.

nodes.label: Translate Tables, Graphs & Equations
nodes.detail: Help students link corresponding values across tables, bar/line graphs, coordinate grids, and algebraic rules so visual patterns match numerical calculations.

nodes.label: Use Manipulatives & Area Models

memoryAids.title: Main idea: Topic + Point
memoryAids.content: Name the topic, then ask what the author says about it across the important details. A main idea is broader than one example but narrower than an unrelated general statement.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

memoryAids.title: Inference bridge
memoryAids.content: TEXT CLUE + RELEVANT KNOWLEDGE = SUPPORTED INFERENCE. State the clue before stating the conclusion; do not treat a guess as evidence.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

memoryAids.title: Context clue scan
memoryAids.content: Read before and after the word. Look for definition, example, contrast, cause, or restatement clues. Substitute the possible meaning and reread.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

memoryAids.title: Source comparison grid
memoryAids.content: Record SHARED FACTS, SOURCE-ONLY DETAILS, VIEWPOINT, and EVIDENCE QUALITY. A difference in emphasis is not automatically a factual contradiction.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

memoryAids.title: Comprehension repair
memoryAids.content: STOP: notice confusion. REREAD: return to the smallest confusing section. RESTATE: explain it in your own words. VERIFY: check the next sentence or text feature.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

memoryAids.title: Fraction operations checkpoint
memoryAids.content: Add or subtract: use common-sized parts, so find a common denominator. Multiply: multiply across and simplify. Divide: multiply by the reciprocal, then verify reasonableness.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

memoryAids.title: Percent triangle
memoryAids.content: PART = PERCENT x WHOLE. Convert the percent to a decimal before multiplying. For percent change, divide the change by the ORIGINAL amount.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

memoryAids.title: Proportion check
memoryAids.content: Keep corresponding units aligned. Find a unit rate or scale both quantities by the same factor. Check that the new ratio is equivalent.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

memoryAids.title: Equation balance
memoryAids.content: Treat an equation like a balanced scale. Apply the same valid operation to both sides, simplify, and substitute the result into the original equation.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

memoryAids.title: Perimeter, area, volume
memoryAids.content: PERIMETER travels around: linear units. AREA covers a surface: square units. VOLUME fills space: cubic units. Match the formula and units to the question.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

memoryAids.title: Data center decision
memoryAids.content: MEAN uses every value and is pulled by outliers. MEDIAN is the middle and resists outliers. MODE is most frequent. Choose the measure that answers the actual question.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

memoryAids.title: Math error-analysis loop
memoryAids.content: ELICIT the student strategy. LOCATE the first incorrect step. REPRESENT the concept. CONNECT the representation to symbols. RECHECK with a new example.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

memoryAids.title: Sentence completeness test
memoryAids.content: Find the subject and complete predicate. Read dependent-clause starters such as because, although, when, and while carefully; they need a main clause.

memoryAids.title: Agreement headword
memoryAids.content: Ignore interrupting prepositional phrases and identify the true subject. Match the verb to that headword, not to a nearby noun.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

memoryAids.title: Comma purpose check
memoryAids.content: Use commas for introductory elements, items in a series, and appropriate clause boundaries. Do not place a comma between a subject and its verb.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

memoryAids.title: Revision before editing
memoryAids.content: REVISION changes meaning, evidence, organization, and clarity. EDITING corrects grammar, usage, punctuation, spelling, and formatting. Revise large structures first.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

memoryAids.title: Paragraph spine
memoryAids.content: TOPIC SENTENCE states the controlling idea. EVIDENCE develops it. EXPLANATION connects evidence to the point. TRANSITION shows the relationship to what comes next.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

memoryAids.title: Claim-evidence-reasoning
memoryAids.content: CLAIM: what you assert. EVIDENCE: relevant and credible support. REASONING: why that evidence makes the claim more convincing. More facts do not replace explanation.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

memoryAids.title: Audience lens
memoryAids.content: Ask what readers already know, what they need to do, and what could confuse them. Adjust vocabulary, detail, organization, headings, examples, and tone.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

memoryAids.title: Feedback that transfers
memoryAids.content: NAME the goal. POINT to exact text. EXPLAIN the effect. OFFER one strategy. RETURN the decision to the writer. Specific feedback builds independence better than rewriting.
memoryAids.reviewNote: A retrieval cue, not a replacement for understanding or current official guidance.

diagramPlacements.learnerPurpose: Guide students through structured reading comprehension support by previewing vocabulary and text features, distinguishing main ideas from supporting details, prompting context-clue and inference checks, and building evidence-based summaries.

Support students in making evidence-based inferences and unlocking unfamiliar vocabulary by gathering explicit textual clues, weighing competing conclusions against overstatements, combining context clues with word parts, and modeling structured think-aloud reasoning.

Help students read informational texts and multiple sources strategically by recognizing organizational patterns, navigating headings and data displays, comparing primary versus secondary viewpoints, and organizing evidence in graphic organizers or source matrices.

Deliver teacher-planned small-group foundational reading practice using phonemic cues, systematic letter-sound and syllable prompts, echo or choral reading for fluency, and objective progress notes for the licensed teacher.

Help students unpack mathematics computation and word problems step by step by identifying known values and goals, modeling with place value, fractions, decimals, or ratios, coaching step-by-step calculation, and checking reasonableness and units.

Guide students through proportional and introductory algebraic reasoning on ParaPro (1755) by preserving multiplicative relationships in ratios and unit rates, simplifying expressions with distributive and like-term rules, solving equations as balanced scales, and coaching through common errors.

Help students solve geometry and measurement tasks accurately on ParaPro (1755) by classifying whether a task asks for perimeter, area, or volume, connecting formulas to perpendicular base and height, reading angles and coordinate grids accurately, and converting units consistently.

Support students in reading data displays and connecting multiple math representations—tables, graphs, manipulatives, area models, and equations—while prompting student reasoning instead of giving away answers.

Verify standard written English conventions on ParaPro (1755) systematically by checking complete independent clauses, aligning subject-verb and pronoun-antecedent agreement, correcting modifiers and parallel structure, and auditing punctuation and capitalization.

Guide students through a clear writing and editing sequence covering complete sentences and punctuation, capitalization/apostrophes/homophones, verb tense and agreement, and coherent paragraph organization while preserving student authorship.

Evaluate and support coherent multi-paragraph writing on ParaPro (1755) by anchoring paragraph unity around topic sentences, linking claims with evidence and explicit reasoning, attributing quotations and paraphrases accurately, and revising whole-document sequence and transitions.

Apply appropriate paraprofessional classroom support practices by implementing teacher-designed lessons and IEP/504 accommodations, using graduated prompting and encouraging feedback, documenting objective observations, and respecting licensed-teacher boundaries.

glossary.definition: Specific central point an author communicates about a general topic across a paragraph or passage, broader than any isolated detail yet narrow enough to fit the text's actual scope.
Instructional sequence moving from explicit modeling to guided practice and independent reading, helping paraprofessionals prompt students with evidence questions without taking over the task.
Logical conclusion formed by pairing explicit textual clues with prior knowledge while verifying that every part of the conclusion is anchored in passage evidence rather than speculation.
Strategy for determining unfamiliar word meanings by combining surrounding sentence signals, such as definitions or contrasts, with analysis of prefixes, roots, and suffixes during reading support.
Framework an author uses to organize ideas, such as sequence, cause and effect, comparison, or problem and solution, signaled by transition words that support student comprehension.
Distinction between firsthand records created during an event and later analyses or summaries, helping students compare viewpoints, purpose, and reliability across informational texts.
Distinguishing word-recognition barriers in phonemic awareness and phonics from fluency or language-comprehension gaps so teacher-directed support addresses the student's actual reading need.
Paraprofessional scope of reinforcing teacher-planned lessons, fading prompts toward student independence, and sharing observations rather than independently diagnosing or redesigning instruction.
Numerical value assigned to a digit by its position in a base-ten numeral, where each place represents ten times the place to its right and anchors regrouping, decimals, and rounding.
Different fraction forms representing the same quantity, generated by multiplying or dividing both numerator and denominator by the same nonzero factor to compare, add, or subtract fractions.
Multiplicative comparison of two quantities that preserves a constant unit rate when both terms are scaled by the same nonzero factor, separating multiplicative from additive reasoning.
Paired mathematical operations that undo one another, such as addition with subtraction and multiplication with division, applied identically to both sides of an equation to isolate an unknown.
Distinct geometric measures representing boundary length in linear units, interior surface coverage in square units, and three-dimensional space in cubic units to prevent formula mix-ups.
Two-dimensional grid formed by perpendicular horizontal (x) and vertical (y) axes meeting at the origin, locating every point uniquely with an ordered pair (x, y) across four quadrants.
Summary statistics describing the center of a data set: the arithmetic average (mean), middle ordered value (median), and most frequent value (mode), interpreted alongside outliers and spread.
Reviewing a student's written work and visual models to pinpoint a specific misconception, such as misaligning place values or adding denominators, before offering a targeted prompt.
Group of words punctuated as a sentence that lacks a subject, a complete verb, or an independent clause, requiring connection to a main clause or addition of missing grammatical elements.
Standard usage principle requiring a verb to match its grammatical subject in number and person, ignoring intervening prepositional phrases and checking compound or indefinite subjects carefully.
Merging choppy or repetitive sentences through coordination or subordination to express logical relationships, such as cause, contrast, or sequence, while preserving the writer's meaning.
Clause structure in which the grammatical subject performs the verb's action rather than receiving it, generally improving clarity, directness, and concision during classroom writing revision.
Focal sentence announcing a paragraph's controlling idea so every supporting detail, example, and transition contributes coherently to the document's overall organization.
Argument framework connecting a clear assertion (claim) with relevant facts or textual details (evidence) and explicit explanation (reasoning) showing why that evidence proves the claim.
Distinguishing higher-order revision of ideas, evidence, and organization from surface-level editing of spelling, punctuation, and grammar so classroom support fits the student's current stage.

glossary.definition: Providing targeted prompts, think-aloud models, and sentence frames so students revise their own drafts rather than having adults rewrite text for them, honoring teacher-directed boundaries.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Guiding main idea, context vocabulary, and text-based inference in 5th grade
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Working under a 5th-grade teacher’s reading plan, outline how you will coach a small group to distinguish the central idea from minor details, unlock vocabulary from context clues, and anchor inferences in textual evidence.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Under the 5th-grade teacher’s small-group plan, you support 4 students reading a 3-paragraph article explaining how urban tree canopies lower summer street temperatures by up to 9 degrees Fahrenheit and absorb stormwater. Three students pick "Trees have green leaves in summer" as the main idea, miss the context clue for "mitigate" ("shade trees help mitigate, or reduce, extreme heat"), and guess inference answers without citing any sentence.
taskParts: A. Identify the specific reading-comprehension breakdown in main idea, context-clue vocabulary, and textual inference shown by the 4 students.

B. Script brief, scaffolded paraprofessional prompts that guide students to locate the central idea, use the appositive clue for "mitigate," and verify inferences in the text without giving away answers.
C. Explain how you will honor teacher-directed paraprofessional boundaries and report concrete observations back to the classroom teacher.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Note that 3 students selected a minor fact ("green leaves") instead of the passage’s overarching benefit of urban canopies, overlooked the explicit synonym clue ("or reduce"), and skipped text verification.

planningFrame.label: Instructional principle
planningFrame.guidance: Use gradual-release questioning aligned to the teacher’s comprehension routine: synthesize repeated paragraph topics for main idea, inspect surrounding appositive clues, and require "point to the line" proof.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Have students underline what all 3 paragraphs discuss (cooling streets by 9 degrees and absorbing stormwater), circle the comma phrase "or reduce" next to "mitigate," and pair each inference with a highlighted sentence.

planningFrame.label: Check & follow-up
planningFrame.guidance: Ask each student to restate the main idea in one sentence using two text facts, then hand the supervising teacher a brief sticky-note tally of who still needed prompting on context clues or citations.

successCriteria: Accurately distinguishes the passage’s main idea (urban tree canopies cool hot streets and manage stormwater) from the minor detail ("green leaves").
Uses the explicit in-sentence appositive clue ("or reduce") to help students derive the meaning of "mitigate" rather than handing out a dictionary definition first.
Models text-dependent questioning ("Which sentence backs up your inference?") so students do the cognitive work instead of passively copying adult answers.
Maintains strict paraprofessional scope by implementing the teacher’s assigned text/plan and sharing objective observational notes rather than redesigning the curriculum or assigning grades.
commonPitfalls: Telling students the correct main idea and definition of "mitigate" directly to finish the worksheet faster.
Swapping the teacher’s assigned article for a different easier passage on your own without teacher approval.
Accepting plausible background-knowledge guesses on inference questions without checking whether the article supports them.
Sending students straight to a glossary before teaching them to notice the "or reduce" context clue right inside the sentence.
sampleOutline: Comprehension snapshot: students confuse a single detail with the central idea, miss an explicit appositive clue ("or reduce"), and make unsupported guesses rather than text-backed inferences.

Guided prompts: ask "What problem do all three paragraphs show trees solving?" to surface cooling and stormwater benefits; prompt students to reread the commas around "mitigate, or reduce" and test substituting "reduce."
Evidence habit: require students to place a finger or highlighter strip on the sentence supporting each inference before sharing aloud with the group.
Teacher handoff: stay within the teacher’s planned text and time block, recording brief student-by-student notes on main-idea vs. context-clue independence for the teacher’s next lesson.
constructedResponseWorkshops.reviewNote: Independent applied case-analysis practice; not an official ETS prompt, rubric, score, pass prediction, or licensure/employment determination. AlloFlow does not score written responses.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Decoding multisyllabic words, building fluency, and using text features in 3rd grade
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Following a 3rd-grade teacher’s guided-reading reinforcement plan, describe how you will coach 3 students on word-part decoding, fluent phrasing, and informational text features while keeping student ownership intact.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Following a 3rd-grade teacher’s small-group plan, you coach 3 students reading a leveled science article on bee pollination featuring bold glossary words, section headings, and a flower diagram. Two students skip words like "unhelpful" and "pollinator" or guess from pictures, read word-by-word at 58 words correct per minute with flat phrasing, and ignore the diagram when asked how pollen moves. One student asks you to read the page aloud for them.
taskParts: A. Diagnose the decoding, fluency, and text-feature habits limiting comprehension for these 3 students without overstepping into formal diagnostic labels.
B. Plan a teacher-aligned support sequence covering morphological/syllable chunking ("un-help-ful", "pol-li-na-tor"), brief repeated-reading fluency practice, and active diagram/glossary use.
C. Respond constructively to the student’s request that you read the whole page for them, and summarize the objective data you will report to the supervising teacher.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Identify picture-guessing on multisyllabic words ("unhelpful", "pollinator"), choppy 58-WCPM word-by-word pacing, skipped diagram/glossary cues, and task-avoidance in asking the adult to read.

planningFrame.label: Instructional principle
planningFrame.guidance: Apply WWC foundational-reading guidance: prompt students to decode through word parts and syllables rather than picture-guessing, model expressive phrasing through echo/choral rereading, and teach text features as meaning tools.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Cover and reveal prefixes, bases, and suffixes ("un" + "help" + "ful"; "pol-li-na-tor"), run a short 2-sentence echo read for phrasing, and have students trace the diagram arrows while checking one bold glossary term.

planningFrame.label: Check & follow-up
planningFrame.guidance: Invite the hesitant student to alternate sentences ("I read one, you read one") so they stay engaged, then share observed decoding patterns and diagram use with the teacher without diagnosing a reading disability.

successCriteria: Replaces picture-guessing with explicit word-part and syllable-chunking prompts ("un-help-ful", "pol-li-na-tor") grounded in print.
Uses brief, supportive fluency routines (echo reading, choral reading, or phrase-scooped rereading of a short excerpt) rather than timed shaming or reading the whole passage for the student.
Directs students to use the section headings, labeled flower diagram, and bold glossary words to answer how pollen travels between blossoms.
Preserves paraprofessional scope by declining to diagnose dyslexia/disabilities and reporting observable reading behaviors directly to the classroom teacher.
commonPitfalls: Reading the entire page aloud for the student to avoid frustration, which removes essential decoding and fluency practice.
Encouraging students to "just look at the picture and guess" when they encounter "unhelpful" or "pollinator."
Telling the teacher or parent that the choppy 58-WCPM readers "probably have dyslexia" instead of reporting factual observations.
Correcting every single miscue instantaneously without giving wait time to self-correct using syllable and word-part strategies.
sampleOutline: Observed needs: students rely on picture guesses on multisyllabic words, read with slow choppy phrasing, overlook diagram/glossary clues, and show reading fatigue.

Decoding & fluency scaffold: guide students to peel off prefix/suffix chunks ("un-help-ful") and blend syllables ("pol-li-na-tor"), then model 2 sentences with natural phrasing followed by choral and partner rereading.
Text-feature integration: pause at the section heading, trace the flower diagram’s labeled path with a finger, and look up one bold word in the glossary to connect visual and written facts.

Boundaries & reporting: offer structured turn-taking ("we will tackle this sentence together") instead of taking over reading, and give the teacher a concise log of missed word parts and fluency response.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Scaffolding fraction addition and percent-discount error analysis in 6th grade
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: During a teacher-assigned 6th-grade rational-number practice block, guide 3 students to uncover and repair misconceptions in fraction addition and percent discounts while keeping computation and estimation in student hands.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: During a 6th-grade math practice block assigned by the teacher, you monitor 3 students solving rational-number problems. On "2/3 + 1/4", two students write "3/7" by adding numerators and denominators straight across. On "A $40 backpack is 15% off; find the sale price", one student subtracts $15 directly to get $25 while another converts 15% to 1.5 and gets a $60 discount. A student asks for the final answers before the bell.
taskParts: A. Verify the correct mathematical solutions and pinpoint the exact conceptual errors behind "3/7", "$25", and the "$60 discount."
B. Sequence visual, benchmark-estimation, and step-by-step questioning supports that help students self-correct both problems without handing over finished answers.
C. Describe how you will close the session responsibly before the bell and communicate student error patterns to the classroom teacher.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Confirm the true answers—2/3 + 1/4 = 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12, and 15% of $40 is $6 giving a $34 sale price—and note the three errors: adding denominators, treating 15% as $15, and converting 15% to 1.5 instead of 0.15.

planningFrame.label: Instructional principle
planningFrame.guidance: Use benchmark estimation and concrete/visual models (fraction strips and 10%-plus-5% percent bars) so students recognize impossible answers (3/7 is less than 1/2; a $60 discount exceeds $40) before recomputing.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Prompt students to estimate 2/3 + 1/4 against 1/2, split thirds and fourths into twelfths to sum 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12, and decompose 15% of $40 into 10% ($4) plus 5% ($2) = $6 off, yielding $40 minus $6 = $34.

planningFrame.label: Check & follow-up
planningFrame.guidance: Decline to give answers just to beat the bell; have students try one fresh transfer item (such as 10% off $30) if time allows, and share the three misconception clusters with the teacher for next-day reteaching.

successCriteria: Computes both problems accurately (2/3 + 1/4 = 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12; 15% of $40 = 0.15 times $40 = $6 discount, sale price = $40 minus $6 = $34).
Uses reasonableness checks ("2/3 is already more than 1/2, so can the sum be 3/7?" and "Can a 15% discount cost more than the entire $40 backpack?") to trigger self-correction.
Scaffolds fraction equivalence with common twelfths and percent conversion (15% = 15/100 = 0.15, or 10% = $4 plus 5% = $2) using student-executed steps.
Refuses to supply completed answers to beat the bell and logs specific rational-number errors for the supervising math teacher.
commonPitfalls: Giving the final answers ("11/12" and "$34") before the bell so students turn in a finished sheet with zero conceptual repair.
Reciting "cross-multiply and butterfly" tricks without explaining why unlike fraction units (thirds and fourths) require equal-sized twelfths.
Overlooking the decimal place-value error (15% = 0.15, not 1.5) or failing to distinguish a $6 discount from the $34 final sale price.
Assigning extra homework or modifying the student’s grade independently instead of relaying error notes to the classroom teacher.
sampleOutline: Math verification & error map: 2/3 + 1/4 = 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12 (not 3/7, which is under 1/2); 15% = 0.15, so 0.15 times $40 = $6 discount and $40 minus $6 = $34 sale price (not $25 or $60 off).
Fraction scaffold: compare 2/3 and 3/7 on a fraction bar to spark cognitive conflict, partition both bars into twelfths, and let students add 8/12 + 3/12 themselves.
Percent scaffold: ask whether 15% means 15 dollars or 15 per 100, model 10% of $40 ($4) plus half of that for 5% ($2) to find $6 off, and verify $40 minus $6 = $34.
Scope & follow-up: prioritize understanding over rushing before the bell, note unfinished items neutrally, and brief the teacher on denominator-addition and percent-decimal confusion.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Supporting proportional reasoning, linear equations, and area versus perimeter in 7th grade
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Under a 7th-grade math teacher’s station directions, coach a small group through three recurring misconceptions—additive ratio thinking, area-versus-perimeter unit confusion, and equation-solving balance errors.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: At a teacher-directed 7th-grade math station, 3 students solve garden-planning problems. Given 3 cups of compost per 2 planter boxes, one student adds 8 to get 11 cups for 10 boxes instead of scaling proportionally. On an 8-foot by 5-foot rectangular bed, another computes 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 and labels the area "26 square feet." On the equation 2x + 4 = 18, a third adds 4 to both sides, getting 2x = 22 and x = 11.
taskParts: A. Verify the accurate solutions (15 cups, 40 square feet vs. 26 feet, and x = 7) and name the underlying misconception in each student’s work.
B. Select concrete representations and guiding questions—ratio tables, grid-array diagrams, and balance/substitution checks—aligned to the teacher’s methods.
C. Explain how you will document station progress for the teacher while respecting paraprofessional instructional boundaries.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Confirm exact values: 3 cups per 2 boxes scales by 5 to 15 cups for 10 boxes (1.5 cups/box); an 8-by-5 rectangle has perimeter 26 feet and area 40 square feet; 2x + 4 = 18 yields 2x = 14 and x = 7.

planningFrame.label: Instructional principle
planningFrame.guidance: Connect proportional scaling to multiplicative unit rates, separate 1D boundary length (feet) from 2D interior coverage (square feet), and treat equation solving as preserving equality verified by substitution.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Build a 2-row ratio table (2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 boxes matched with 3, 6, 9, 12, and 15 cups), sketch an 8-by-5 unit-square grid, and ask the third student to plug x = 11 back into 2(11) + 4 = 26 to discover why subtracting 4 is required.

planningFrame.label: Check & follow-up
planningFrame.guidance: Have each student verify their revised answer with units or substitution, then deliver a brief station summary noting which misconceptions resolved with visual prompts and which need teacher follow-up.

successCriteria: Verifies all three solutions accurately: 15 cups of compost (unit rate 1.5 cups/box), 40 square feet for area versus 26 feet for perimeter, and x = 7 for 2x + 4 = 18.
Diagnoses additive thinking in ratios (+8 instead of times 5), formula/unit conflation in perimeter vs. area, and using addition instead of the inverse operation (subtraction) to undo +4.
Uses visual and self-checking tools (ratio table, 8-by-5 grid sketch, and plugging x = 11 vs. x = 7 into 2x + 4) so students catch their own errors.
Stays within the teacher’s station framework, never introducing conflicting shortcut rules or altering official station grades.
commonPitfalls: Accepting "26 square feet" as almost right without separating linear feet (fencing around the edge) from square feet (covering the soil surface).
Solving 2x + 4 = 18 on the student’s paper yourself instead of letting substitution (2 times 11 plus 4 equals 26, not 18) expose the error.
Explaining ratios only with abstract cross-multiplication while the student still believes adding 8 to both quantities preserves the ratio.
Inventing a brand-new homework worksheet on your own rather than reporting the station’s misconception log to the teacher.
sampleOutline: Verified math & error diagnosis: 3/2 = 15/10 (additive +8 error gave 11); 8 ft by 5 ft has area 40 sq ft and perimeter 26 ft; 2x + 4 = 18 yields 2x = 14 and x = 7 (adding 4 gave 2x = 22 and x = 11).

Proportional & geometry scaffolds: extend a ratio table by pairs (2 boxes/3 cups up to 10 boxes/15 cups) and draw an 8-by-5 grid so students contrast 26 boundary segments (ft) against 40 tiled squares (sq ft).

Equation-check scaffold: prompt the student to substitute x = 11 into 2x + 4 (getting 26, not 18), identify the inverse of adding 4 as subtracting 4, solve 2x = 14 to get x = 7, and re-verify 2(7) + 4 = 18.
Teacher coordination: keep the teacher’s station sequence intact and pass along concise notes on multiplicative scaling, unit labels, and inverse operations.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Coaching grammar, sentence boundaries, and dangling modifiers without rewriting student work
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Following a 7th-grade ELA teacher’s editing checklist, plan a focused paraprofessional writing conference that helps a student spot and revise agreement, comma-splice, modifier, and usage errors while retaining full authorship.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Following the 7th-grade teacher’s editing checklist, you conference with a student over this draft: "The box of science supplies were sitting by the door, we carried them to lab. Walking quickly down the hall, the beakers nearly slipped out of my hands. Their is two charts we need to finish before Friday." The student asks you to fix every error with a red pen so they can submit a clean draft immediately.
taskParts: A. Catalog each grammar, usage, and sentence-structure error in the 3-sentence draft and explain why each breaks standard conventions or clarity.
B. Prioritize 2 high-leverage targets from the teacher’s checklist and script guiding questions that help the student hear and revise the sentences themselves.
C. Address the student’s request for a red-pen rewrite while upholding paraprofessional scope and preserving student ownership.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Identify all four issues: singular subject "box" paired with plural "were", a comma splice plus ambiguous "them" ("by the door, we carried them"), a dangling modifier ("beakers" walking down the hall), and homophone/agreement error ("Their is two charts").

planningFrame.label: Instructional principle
planningFrame.guidance: Keep the pencil or keyboard in the student’s hands, focus on 1–2 checklist patterns at a time, and use read-aloud and concrete meaning questions so the writer learns transferable editing habits.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Have the student cross out the prepositional phrase "of science supplies" to match "box was", split the comma splice with a period or ", so", ask "Who was walking down the hall?" to revise to "I nearly dropped the beakers", and check "There are two charts."

planningFrame.label: Check & follow-up
planningFrame.guidance: Ask the student to read their revised paragraph aloud to check flow, mark completed checklist boxes together, and note recurring agreement/homophone patterns for the supervising ELA teacher.

successCriteria: Accurately spots all four errors: subject-verb agreement ("The box of science supplies was"), comma splice/pronoun clarity ("by the door. We carried the supplies"), dangling modifier ("Walking quickly down the hall, I nearly dropped the beakers"), and homophone/agreement ("There are two charts").
Declines to red-pen rewrite the draft and keeps all editing decisions and physical revisions under the student’s control.
Uses targeted meaning-based questions (such as "Who is doing the walking?" and "What single noun is sitting by the door?") tied directly to the teacher’s checklist.
Paces feedback so the student is not overwhelmed and communicates observed editing needs back to the classroom teacher.
commonPitfalls: Taking the red pen and rewriting all three sentences yourself to save time, which violates student authorship and hides true mastery from the teacher.
Missing the subject-verb agreement trap because plural "supplies" sits right next to "were", or fixing "Their" to "There" while leaving "is two charts" uncorrected.
Overlooking the dangling modifier ("the beakers" appearing to walk down the hall) because the sentence sounds casual at a quick glance.
Giving an informal grade estimate or rewriting the teacher’s editing rubric during the conference.
sampleOutline: Error audit: (1) change "box of science supplies were" to "was"; (2) split the comma splice and clarify vague "them"; (3) fix the dangling modifier by naming "I" right after the opening phrase; (4) change "Their is two charts" to "There are two charts."
Authorship boundary: kindly explain that the checklist is for building their editing eye, so they keep the pen while you coach one sentence at a time.

Guided coaching: read aloud to hear the comma-splice pause, bracket "of science supplies" to find singular "box", ask "Can beakers walk down a hall?" to fix the modifier, and review the "there/their" anchor chart for "There are two charts."
Closure & teacher note: have the student re-read the polished draft for clarity and log subject-verb agreement and homophone practice needs for the ELA teacher.
